timeline.title: Born beside a hospital for the poor
timeline.text: Fyodor was born on 11 November 1821 (30 October in the old Russian calendar), the second child of Dr Mikhail Dostoevsky. The family lived on the grounds of the Mariinsky Hospital for the Poor, and as a boy he met the patients while playing in its gardens. His nanny told him fairy tales and legends, and his mother taught him to read from the Bible.

timeline.title: His mother dies
timeline.text: His mother died of tuberculosis. Around the same time, he and his older brother Mikhail were sent to Saint Petersburg to prepare for military engineering school, giving up the studies they loved.

timeline.title: An engineer who wanted to write
timeline.text: He entered the Nikolayev Military Engineering Institute. He had little interest in mathematics or the army and preferred drawing, architecture and books. A classmate said no student looked less like a soldier, but he was respected for standing up for newcomers.

timeline.title: His father dies
timeline.text: News came that his father had died while Fyodor was away at school. The official cause was a stroke. A neighbour accused the family's serfs of murder, but they were found not guilty at trial. Stories of an early seizure at this time come from later accounts now thought unreliable.

timeline.title: Engineer by day, translator by night
timeline.text: He took a job as a lieutenant engineer. That summer his first published work appeared: a Russian translation of Balzac's novel Eugenie Grandet. His translations earned little, and money troubles pushed him to try writing a novel of his own.

timeline.title: Poor Folk makes his name
timeline.text: His first novel, Poor Folk, told in letters between two poor people, was published and became a success. His roommate Grigorovich had carried the manuscript to the poet Nekrasov, who showed it to the powerful critic Belinsky. Belinsky called it Russia's first "social novel". Dostoevsky soon asked to resign from the army so he could write.

timeline.title: The Double and harsh reviews
timeline.text: His second novel, The Double, came out just two weeks later and was badly reviewed, including by Belinsky. Several short stories that followed, such as White Nights, also met a cool reception, and he struggled with money and poor health.

timeline.title: The Petrashevsky Circle
timeline.text: He began attending the Friday meetings of the Petrashevsky Circle, a group that discussed banned books, censorship and ending serfdom. Sources differ on the year: the main Wikipedia article says 1846, the article on the Circle says 1847. In 1848 a member named Speshnev formed a secret society inside the group, and Dostoevsky joined it, though he had doubts about its aims.

timeline.title: Before the firing squad
timeline.text: Arrested in April 1849, he spent eight months in the Peter and Paul Fortress, accused of reading and passing on a banned letter by Belinsky. The court sentenced the group to death. On a December morning they were taken to Semyonov Place and the first three men were placed before the firing squad. Then a messenger arrived: the tsar had changed the sentence to hard labour. The reprieve had been planned in advance as a deliberate deception. Sources give the date as 22 or 23 December.

timeline.title: Four years in a prison camp
timeline.text: After a long sleigh journey through winter, he reached the hard labour camp at Omsk in Siberia. On the way, at Tobolsk, the wives of earlier exiles gave the prisoners copies of the New Testament, and it was the only book he was allowed. He was kept in shackles, the barracks were filthy and cold, and his health suffered. Most other prisoners came to respect him.

timeline.title: Out of prison, into the army
timeline.text: Released from the camp, he was sent to serve as a soldier in Semipalatinsk. He wrote to his brother asking for books by Kant, Hegel and historians. He tutored local children and made friends, including Baron Wrangel, who had witnessed the mock execution.

timeline.title: A first marriage
timeline.text: After a letter of apology for his part in the circles, he was allowed to publish and to marry, though police watched him for the rest of his life. He married Maria Isaeva, a widow he had met in Semipalatinsk. He later wrote that they were not happy together but could not stop loving each other.

timeline.title: Home after ten years
timeline.text: Released from the army because of poor health, he was allowed back to European Russia. In Tver he saw his brother Mikhail for the first time in ten years, then returned to Saint Petersburg, exactly ten years after he had been sent away.

timeline.title: The House of the Dead
timeline.text: He began publishing The House of the Dead, a novel built from his years in the Omsk camp. It ran from 1860 to 1862 and was the first published novel about Russian prisons. With Mikhail he also founded the magazine Vremya (Time), where his novel Humiliated and Insulted appeared.

timeline.title: First journey west
timeline.text: He made his first trip to Western Europe, visiting Germany, Paris, London and Italy. In London he met Alexander Herzen and saw the Crystal Palace, which he came to see as a symbol of soulless modern progress. He wrote about the trip in Winter Notes on Summer Impressions.

timeline.title: The roulette tables
timeline.text: On a second trip he gambled at Wiesbaden and Baden-Baden and lost nearly all his money. He had written that the secret was to stay calm and never get excited, but within a week he had lost his winnings and had to ask his family for help. He gambled on and off until 1871.

timeline.title: Notes from Underground
timeline.text: He published Notes from Underground in his new magazine Epoch. Told by a bitter, isolated man, it is often called one of the first works of existentialist literature.

timeline.title: A year of loss
timeline.text: His wife Maria and his brother Mikhail both died in 1864. He became the only parent of his stepson and took on the support of his brother's family. When Epoch failed, his debts grew, and only help from friends and relatives kept him from bankruptcy.

timeline.title: Crime and Punishment
timeline.text: The first parts of Crime and Punishment appeared in The Russian Messenger and ran through the year. It follows Raskolnikov, a poor former student who talks himself into a murder and is then torn apart by guilt. It is often called one of the greatest works of world literature.

timeline.title: The Gambler in 26 days
timeline.text: To pay debts he had signed a hard contract with the publisher Stellovsky: deliver a new novel by 1 November 1866, or Stellovsky could publish all his works for nine years without paying him. With a month left he had not started. A friend suggested a stenographer, and from 4 October Anna Snitkina took down his dictation in shorthand and copied it out. They finished The Gambler on 30 October, after 26 days. Sources give her age as 19 or 20.

timeline.title: Marriage to Anna
timeline.text: He married Anna Snitkina in Trinity Cathedral. She became his partner in work as well as life, taking down his novels and later running the business side of his books.

timeline.title: Fleeing debt, losing again
timeline.text: The couple left for a delayed honeymoon in Germany. The 7,000 rubles from Crime and Punishment did not cover their debts, and Anna sold her valuables to pay for the trip. In Baden-Baden he quarrelled with the writer Turgenev and again lost heavily at roulette. A trip planned for three months lasted over four years.

timeline.title: The Idiot
timeline.text: The Idiot began to appear in January 1868. Its hero, Prince Myshkin, is a truly good man in a selfish world. Through him Dostoevsky told the story of a man reprieved in front of a firing squad, drawn from his own morning in 1849. He finished the novel in Florence in January 1869.

timeline.title: A daughter born and lost
timeline.text: Their first child, Sofya, was born in Geneva. She died of pneumonia three months later. Anna remembered her husband weeping in despair. A second daughter, Lyubov, was born in Dresden in 1869.

timeline.title: The last time at the tables
timeline.text: He made a final visit to a gambling hall in Wiesbaden. Anna said he stopped gambling after this, but whether he gave it up completely is debated. In July the family came home to Saint Petersburg after more than four years abroad.

timeline.title: Publishing their own books
timeline.text: Demons, a novel about a group of young radicals, inspired by a real political murder in 1869, came out as a book from their own Dostoevsky Publishing Company. Anna ran the finances, sold copies from their flat and took only cash. It sold about 3,000 copies. The same month he began writing A Writer's Diary in the magazine The Citizen.

timeline.title: The Adolescent
timeline.text: He finished The Adolescent, a novel about a young man and the father who barely knew him. Fathers and sons became a key theme of his last books. His son Alexey was born that August.

timeline.title: A Writer's Diary
timeline.text: He published A Writer's Diary as his own periodical: essays and a few stories on society, faith, politics and ethics. It sold more than twice as many copies as his earlier books. Readers wrote to him and visited him in large numbers.

timeline.title: The death of Alyosha
timeline.text: His three-year-old son Alexey, called Alyosha, died after an epileptic seizure. Later that year Dostoevsky visited the Optina Monastery. He named the gentle hero of his next novel Alyosha.

timeline.title: The Brothers Karamazov
timeline.text: His last novel began to appear in The Russian Messenger and ran until November 1880. It asks big questions about God, free will and morality through the story of three brothers and their father. He wrote much of it in Staraya Russa, which inspired the setting. It is widely seen as one of the supreme achievements of world literature.

timeline.title: The Pushkin Speech
timeline.text: At the unveiling of a monument to the poet Pushkin in Moscow, he gave a speech that moved the audience deeply. It was met with thunderous applause, and even his old rival Turgenev embraced him. Critics on both left and right attacked it afterwards.

timeline.title: Death in Saint Petersburg
timeline.text: After several lung haemorrhages, he died on 9 February 1881 (28 January in the old calendar). He asked for the parable of the Prodigal Son to be read to his children. He was buried in the Tikhvin Cemetery at the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. Reports of the funeral crowd differ widely, from 40,000 to more than 100,000.

timeline.title: Into English, and the world
timeline.text: Constance Garnett's English translation of The Brothers Karamazov appeared in 1912, followed by Crime and Punishment in 1914. Her versions spread his novels across the English-speaking world. Today his books have been translated into more than 170 languages, and writers and thinkers from Chekhov to Camus have learned from him.

works.title: Poor Folk
works.text: His first novel, told in letters between two poor distant cousins. Belinsky called it Russia's first social novel, and it made Dostoevsky famous overnight.

works.title: The Double
works.text: A short novel about a clerk who meets a man exactly like himself. Poorly received at the time.

works.title: The House of the Dead
works.text: A fictionalised memoir of life in a Siberian prison camp, based on his four years at Omsk. The first published novel about Russian prisons.

works.title: Vremya and Epoch
works.text: Magazines he ran with his brother Mikhail. Vremya was shut down by the government, and the failure of Epoch left him deep in debt.

works.title: Notes from Underground
works.text: The confession of a bitter, isolated man who rebels against the idea that people act only by reason. Often called one of the first existentialist works.

works.title: Crime and Punishment
works.text: A poor student convinces himself that a murder can be justified, then is torn apart by conscience. The first great novel of his mature years.

works.title: The Gambler
works.text: A short novel about a young tutor drawn into roulette at a German resort, drawing on his own gambling. Dictated to Anna Snitkina and finished in 26 days to meet a deadline.

works.title: The Idiot
works.text: Prince Myshkin, a deeply good and open-hearted man, is mistaken for a fool by the people around him. Includes the story of a man reprieved before a firing squad.

works.title: Demons (The Possessed)
works.text: A dark satire and tragedy about a small town thrown into chaos by young radicals, inspired by a real political murder of 1869.

works.title: The Dostoevsky Publishing Company
works.text: The family's own publishing business, run by Anna, which sold his books directly and helped them climb out of debt.

works.title: The Adolescent
works.text: A young man's story of finding his way and his difficult bond with the father who barely knew him.

works.title: A Writer's Diary
works.text: A one-man periodical of essays and stories on Russian life, faith, politics and ethics. It outsold his earlier books.

works.title: The Brothers Karamazov
works.text: His last and largest novel: three brothers, their father and a murder, with famous chapters such as Rebellion and The Grand Inquisitor.

works.title: The Pushkin Speech
works.text: A speech in Moscow on the poet Pushkin and the Russian spirit, one of the great public moments of his life.
